people.label: Thomas Townsend Brown
people.sub: Electrostatic-propulsion inventor; five patents; subject of a 1953 FBI fraud inquiry
people.narrative:
Thomas Townsend Brown is the technical origin point on which the entire electrogravitics thread hangs, and the useful thing this board can do with him is separate what he patented from what was later written about him. The patents are real and were read off the USPTO's own image server: US 1,974,483 ELECTROSTATIC MOTOR (1934), US 2,207,576 (1940), US 2,417,347 VIBRATION DAMPER (1947, assigned by mesne assignments to Lockheed Aircraft Corporation), US 2,949,550 ELECTROKINETIC APPARATUS (1960) and US 3,187,206 ELECTROKINETIC APPARATUS (1965). None of them claims gravity control. The 1934 patent claims 'a method of producing force or motion by applying and maintaining high potential electro-static charges'; the 1965 patent opens 'This invention relates to an electrical device for producing thrust by the direct operation of electrical fields' and is explicit that the reaction appears in the surrounding medium and, in vacuum, on the walls of the chamber. That is an electrostatic-thrust claim. The word 'electrogravitics' appears in none of them.

Project Winterhaven is real and does not say what the secondary literature says it says. The 66-page proposal, 'A PROPOSAL FOR JOINT SERVICES RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT CONTRACT, THE TOWNSEND BROWN FOUNDATION', does propose research on 'the control of gravitation' and lists 'electrified disc airfoils' among results to date. But the words 'saucer', 'interceptor', 'Mach' and 'Air Force' appear in it zero times. The saucer-as-USAF-interceptor framing belongs to the 1956 Aviation Studies (International) report 'Electrogravitics Systems', not to Winterhaven, and that report has no catalogue record anywhere WorldCat indexes.

The provenance that matters most is the one the enthusiast literature omits. Brown's own FBI file records the Winterhaven pitch inside a Fraud Against the Government inquiry: the LEADS section directs the Washington Field Office to 'ascertain from appropriate defense agencies the nature of any overtures made by BROWN' and to 'determine any possible violation of the [F]AG Statute'. The same file carries named informants describing the apparatus as a relabelled stock-market predicting machine, one of them 'confident this flying saucer thing is a phony'. A node on Brown that carries the patents without that is not an honest node.

people.label: Philip J. Corso
people.sub: Lt. Col., US Army; Chief, Foreign Technology Division, OCRD, 18 Apr - 18 Jul 1962
people.narrative:
Corso is the case where the primary record is both stronger and weaker than the claim made for him, and a node is the only place a reader sees both halves. His own DA Form 66, released by US Army Reserve Personnel Command in April 1998, puts the Army's Foreign Technology Division in his service record: staff officer in the division from 20 July 1961, then 'Chief Foreign Technology Div, OCRD USA' from 18 April to 18 July 1962 -- three months. The same form places him at Fort Riley, Kansas from 21 April 1947, which covers the alleged 6 July 1947 observation, and records him as an Intelligence Staff Officer on the Operations Coordinating Board in Washington from 24 February 1954 to 1957.

His 322-page FBI release is the other half. Searched in full, the words UFO, flying saucer, unidentified, Roswell, extraterrestrial and saucer appear zero times. What the file does contain is independent corroboration of the OCB posting from a source that is not Corso: in 1955 Gen. Arthur S. Trudeau told the FBI that 'Colonel Philip Corso, then assigned to the Operations Coordinating Board, would be in a position to elaborate' on a list of alleged Fabian Socialists, 'as he, Corso, had actually accumulated the information'. It also contains a 1964 episode in which Corso was found to be the source of a rumour that Oswald had been a paid FBI informant, and in which he 'emphasized the fact that his allegations had been strictly deductions and had no basis in fact'.

One line in his sworn statement does not survive his own service record. The affidavit says he 'was a member of President Eisenhower's National Security Council'. The DA Form 66 records the Operations Coordinating Board, which reported to the NSC and was not the NSC. That is a documentable overstatement in a sworn document, and this board carries it because the same record that supplies his strongest corroboration supplies it.

people.label: Roscoe H. Hillenkoetter
people.sub: First Director of Central Intelligence, May 1947 - October 1950; NICAP board member 1960
people.narrative:
The first Director of Central Intelligence went on the public record in 1960 saying that the objects were 'operating under intelligent control' and asking Congress to investigate, and the documents that establish it are held by the Central Intelligence Agency itself. A Worcester Gazette clipping of 1 June 1960, filed in CIA records and released in 2014, reports him declaring: 'The unknown objects are operating under intelligent control. It is imperative that we learn where the UFO's (unidentified flying objects) come from and what their purpose is.' The same clipping gives his tenure as DCI, May 1947 to October 1950, and reports that he wanted a congressional investigation. A second CIA-held clipping, an Enquirer editorial of 4 March 1960, independently records him as a board member of NICAP who 'has referred his conclusions to the Senate Space Committee, requesting an investigation' -- while itself disagreeing with him.

None of that requires MJ-12, and this board does not route him through it. The purported 1948 Hillenkoetter-to-Truman memo shown to be an emulation of a Marshall-to-Roosevelt letter is a claim about a document, not about the man, and nothing above depends on it. A negative finding points the same way as the Corso file: the National Security Archive's mirror of the FBI files on Hillenkoetter contains, across the sections searched, zero occurrences of NICAP, flying saucer, unidentified flying, Keyhoe, or the year 1960. His FBI file is not a UFO file.

The structural point is the ordering. A former DCI publicly contradicting the Air Force's public position, while sitting on the board of the organisation pressing for hearings, is a fact about the disclosure apparatus that the board should reach directly rather than through somebody else's narrative about a forgery.

people.label: Robert I. Sarbacher
people.sub: Microwave engineer; Dean of the Graduate Division, Georgia Tech; author of the 1983 Steinman letter
people.narrative:
The board already leans on Sarbacher second-hand, through Wilbert Smith, and a node is the only place the distinction that matters can be put where a reader sees it: he says in his own signed letter that he was invited to the meetings and did not attend them. The letter is real. Two typed pages on Washington Institute of Technology letterhead, dated 29 November 1983, addressed to William Steinman, signed, with Steinman's handwritten receipt note 'Received 12-5-83'. In it Sarbacher says John von Neumann and Vannevar Bush 'definitely' were involved and 'I think Dr. Robert Oppenheimer also'; that 'I could not personally attend the meetings'; that materials 'reported to have come from flying saucer crashes were extremely light and very tough'; and that he 'got the impression these aliens were constructed like certain insects we have observed on earth.' Everything about a Wright Field meeting, and everything Eric Walker is said to have said, is not in this letter.

Two problems are visible on the document's own face. Sarbacher writes of 'My association with the Research and Development Board under Doctor Compton during the Eisenhower administration' -- the RDB was a Truman-era body abolished in June 1953, five months into Eisenhower's first term, and Karl T. Compton chaired it in the late 1940s. At about 76 he is conflating administrations in the most-quoted paragraph of the document. And his postscript, asking Steinman to check the spelling of Bush's name, is omitted from the typed transcript bound into the same PDF, so anyone quoting the transcript is quoting an abridged letter.

His credentials are not in doubt: the title page of his 1943 Wiley textbook names him 'Robert I. Sarbacher, Sc.D., Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering, Illinois Institute of Technology'. What is in doubt is the RDB consultancy the secondary literature attaches to him, for which no primary record was found, and the provenance of the letter itself, which reaches this board through an advocacy publisher's scan rather than an institutional archive.

people.label: Eric H. Wang
people.sub: Chief, Special Studies Office, Installations Division, Air Materiel Command; later Chief, Structures Division, AFSWC Kirtland
people.narrative:
Eric H. Wang is on this board because he is documented, and the documentation is the point: it establishes a named Air Materiel Command office chief at Wright Field who moved to Kirtland, and it establishes nothing else. Four Operation UPSHOT-KNOTHOLE structures reports at DTIC name him identically: 'Eric H. Wang, Chief, Special Studies Office, who was the technical and scientific monitor for the Air Force Program', with Arthur Stansel and Mrs. Maisie G. Ridgeway in the same section. The Project 3.1 report records that responsibility for the six projects transferred 'from the Special Studies Office, Installations Division, Air Materiel Command to Blast Effects Research, Mechanics Branch, Aeronautical Research Laboratory, Wright Air Development Center, on 15 November 1954'. A 1960 report names him 'Eric H. Wang, Chief, Structures Division' at Headquarters Research Directorate, Air Force Special Weapons Center, Kirtland Air Force Base.

His documented role is atomic blast effects on structures. That is a real and sensitive job at Kirtland and it explains his presence there without needing anything else. Nothing in any of these reports touches UAP, recovered materiel, reverse engineering, Kissinger or Schauberger, and no document supporting an Austrian birth was found. Those claims are not on this board at any tier, and this node exists partly to say so.

Three corrections travel with him. The printed name of the office is the Special Studies Office, inside the Installations Division of Air Materiel Command, not the 'Office of Special Studies'. His middle initial is H. The colleague is Arthur Stansel, not Stancil -- and the Project 3.5 report tracks him onward to the Landing Gear Development Section, Equipment Laboratory, Wright Air Development Center.

people.label: Louis Witten
people.sub: General relativist; first researcher hired by RIAS, Inc., the Glenn L. Martin Company's research institute
people.narrative:
Louis Witten is on this board for one documented fact and its context: in January 1957 he attended the Chapel Hill conference on the role of gravitation in physics as a representative of RIAS, Inc., Baltimore. The participants list of the conference report prints it plainly -- 'Witten, L. | RIAS, Inc., Baltimore' -- immediately above 'Bass, R.W. | RIAS, Inc., Baltimore'. His contribution, with R. W. Bass, was 'Some Remarks on Cosmological Models'. The report's own designation is WADC Technical Report 57-216 and it exists because of a conference funding agreement with the Wright Air Development Center, which is to say an Air Force body paid for the meeting at which an aerospace prime's research institute discussed gravitation.

What is documented about his work is classical general relativity, not gravity control. The conference participants themselves recorded a concern about 'the absolute necessity to avoid identification with so-called anti-gravity research', and nothing read in this pass shows RIAS producing gravity-control results. The board carries him as the hire that establishes what RIAS actually was, and it does not carry the claim that George Trimble recruited him -- the one source that could be opened says Witten approached Bryce DeWitt to recruit DeWitt, and the oral history that would settle the direction refuses this environment.

people.label: George S. Trimble
people.sub: Glenn L. Martin Company executive; proposed RIAS as an industrial institute for advanced study
people.narrative:
RIAS was Trimble's idea and gravity was explicitly its subject, and both facts come off his own dated letter. Writing to Bryce DeWitt on 10 June 1955 he opens: 'During a recent conversation with Mr. George Rideout, president of Roger Babson's Gravity Research Foundation, we were commiserating on the unfortunate state of the affairs that knowledgable folks do not wish to get mixed up in the field of gravity research.' He continues: 'It occurred to us some time ago that our industry was vitally concerned with gravity ... At least one category of the things one must study, when he desires to bring space flight to reality, is the laws of nature surrounding the force of gravity.' He described the proposed body as an 'industrial version of the Institute for Advanced Study'.

That is an aerospace prime's executive, in 1955, in writing, saying his industry needed gravity research and that respectable people would not touch it -- which is a documented statement of exactly the reputational mechanism this board maps elsewhere. Martin money also reached the university side: Trimble and the Glenn L. Martin Company bought a Founder's Membership in the Institute of Field Physics for $5,000 and offered to help solicit more.

The industrial and academic halves were deliberately kept apart, and the source says why. The Martin company's institute was 'industry-sponsored, and not ensconced in a university', while the Institute of Field Physics was placed inside UNC 'so as to avoid the conflict that physicists felt working in an industrial setting.' Note what is not carried here: no document read states that Trimble recruited Louis Witten, and this board draws no such edge.

entities.label: GAO accession 130581 - Controls Over Classified Documents for a Special Access Program at Lockheed Corporation
entities.sub: GAO testimony, 24 July 1986, House Energy and Commerce, Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations
entities.desc:
On 24 July 1986 the General Accounting Office told a congressional subcommittee that a prime contractor's special-access document control had failed, and in the same statement explained that the body which would ordinarily have inspected it had been excluded from doing so since 1965. That conjunction is this board's structural argument, documented and dated. The cover page reads: 'STATEMENT OF MARTIN M FERBER, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, NATIONAL SECURITY AND INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS DIVISION, BEFORE THE SUBCOMMITTEE ON OVERSIGHT AND INVESTIGATIONS, HOUSE COMMITTEE ON ENERGY AND COMMERCE, ON CONTROLS OVER CLASSIFIED DOCUMENTS FOR A SPECIAL ACCESS PROGRAM AT LOCKHEED CORPORATION'. The venue is worth noting: not a defence committee.

The numbers are exact and the popular version of them is wrong. Lockheed reported 1,460 discrepancies in an inventory of about 40,000 secret and top-secret items. As of 19 July 1986 it had completed investigation on 235 of them; 224 were 'later accounted for' and 11 were unresolved -- 7 inadvertently destroyed and 4 not located. The 46 destroyed and the 17 transferred out of the company sit inside the 224 that were accounted for, not outside them. The genuinely unaccounted-for total is 11.

GAO explains the carve-out in its own words: special access contracts are 'carved out of the Defense Investigative Service's periodic inspection program', a 1965 decision, and by 1983 GAO estimated 'there probably were several thousand such contracts'. Its closing sentence is the finding: 'it appears inconsistent to us to establish a special access program because of security considerations and then afford it less document protection than normal classified programs.' The companion letter report to the Secretary of Defense, GAO/NSIAD-86-191 of 7 August 1986, goes further and names the plant the testimony would not.

entities.label: Defense Investigative Service

entities.desc:
The Defense Investigative Service is the body whose absence the board keeps having to explain. It conducted the periodic industrial security inspections of cleared contractor facilities -- including, GAO says in terms, other contracts at Lockheed -- and it was excluded from special access programs by a Department of Defense decision in 1965. GAO's own vocabulary preserves the mechanism: special access contracts are called carve-out contracts 'because they are carved out of the Defense Investigative Service's periodic inspection program'.

Two GAO findings bracket what that exclusion cost. In February 1983, GAO/GGD-83-43 recommended improvements in DoD oversight of carve-out contracts and DoD refused, on stated grounds including that 'access by Service inspectors would proliferate access beyond the minimum number of persons necessary'. In August 1986, after the Lockheed document-control failure, GAO told the Secretary of Defense that the failure 'may not have occurred if the Defense Investigative Service had been permitted to conduct semiannual inspections of the contract, as it does with other contracts at Lockheed.' The board carries DIS because the argument it makes about custody is not that oversight failed but that oversight was structurally absent, and this is the office that was absent from it.

entities.label: 1127th USAF Field Activities Group
entities.sub: Air Force intelligence unit running Project BLUE FLY and Project MOON DUST under its Foreign Materiel Program
entities.desc:
This is the custody chain stated by the unit that ran it, about itself, in a document classified SECRET at the time. The 1127th USAF Field Activities Group's own semiannual history for 1 January to 30 June 1967, document number AFNIABA 014-67, prepared by Anita H. Beasey and approved by Colonel Rudolph C. Koller, Jr., lists on its contents page, under FOREIGN MATERIEL PROGRAM: 'Project BLUE FLY' (p.29), 'MIG-17 Exploitation' (p.29), 'Project MOON DUST' (p.30). The board has carried the Moon Dust and Blue Fly relationship as an inference; here it is an organisational fact, printed in a table of contents.

The BLUE FLY entry describes the mechanism end to end. After the air battle of 7 April 1967, three MIG-21s downed over Jordan were exploited by Detachment 3 of the Foreign Technology Division, and the Staff Operations Branch 'coordinated requirements necessary to deploy the FTD exploitation personnel and to airlift personnel and parts from site of acquisition to Wright-Patterson AFB. The take consisted of approximately three tons of aircraft parts and armament.' The Joint Chiefs had approved a one-year extension of Force/Activity Designator I priority for short-notice BLUE FLY airlift. That is recovery, transport priority and a named terminus, in one paragraph.

The MOON DUST entry, and the companion history of the Assistant Chief of Staff, Intelligence for July to December 1967, carry the figures usually quoted as recoveries. They are not recoveries. Both documents say the unit was NOTIFIED by SPADATS of DEORBITS -- 37 Soviet objects in the first half of 1967, and 49 Soviet plus 17 US objects in the second. Deorbit notification is the tasking trigger; recovery is a separate act neither document counts.

entities.desc:
The Research and Development Board sat at the top of the American defence research structure for the exact six years in which the legacy programme is alleged to have been established, and its statutory life is fully documented. The National Archives' finding aid for Record Group 330 states it was 'Established as the Research and Development Board by the National Security Act of 1947 (61 Stat. 495), July 26, 1947. The same aid lists its surviving records, including 'Minutes of meetings of the Executive Council, 1946-50' and 'Records of the Committee on Technical Information, 1946-53'.

Truman's published letter to Vannevar Bush of 25 September 1947 gives the predecessor relationship in the President's own words: 'I am happy to know that you are willing to continue in the public service as Chairman of the Research and Development Board created by the National Security Act of 1947 ... Since V-J Day you have continued to render valuable service as chairman of the Joint Research and Development Board set up by the Secretaries of War and Navy.' The RDB is a 1947 statutory body and its predecessor the JRDB is a post-V-J Day creation of the two service secretaries -- so no earlier than September 1945.

What this node does NOT carry is the Sarbacher consultancy. It is the destination every MJ-12 and Wilbert Smith thread points at, and no primary record for it was found. It is carried at Tier 3 on the Sarbacher node, where it belongs, and no edge is drawn from here.

entities.label: Aurora (FY1986-FY1987 procurement line)
entities.sub: A classified programme made visible by the Pentagon's own unclassified P-1 document, February 1985
entities.desc:
Aurora belongs on this board as budget mechanics and nothing else. It is a documented instance of a classified programme becoming visible through the Pentagon's own unclassified paperwork and then being denied on the record by the service that published it -- a mechanism the board argues about elsewhere, here with a date and a document.

The Washington Post of 8 February 1985, preserved in the CIA's reading room as CIA-RDP90-00965R000807470050-4, reports: 'The Pentagon has said in a public document that it wants $2.3 billion for an Air Force plane called Aurora but responded yesterday that the plane -- if it really is a plane -- is classified.' It names the mechanism precisely: 'The secrecy cloak slipped off the spending plans for Aurora when the Pentagon compiled its unclassified shopping list, known as the P1 document. The P stands for procurement.' The figures in the body are exact: 'Spending for Aurora, according to this public document, shoots up from zero this fiscal year to $80 million in fiscal 1986 to $2.27 billion in fiscal 1987.' The $2.3 billion in the headline is the article's own rounding; the board uses $2.27bn.

The denial is in the same paragraph: 'Reminded that Aurora has been put in the public domain by the Pentagon, an Air Force spokesman said his orders still were to say only: It's a classified program.' This is five years before the Aviation Week story that usually gets the credit. No craft claim and no recovery claim attaches here: the article's own sources point at Stealth.

entities.label: AFIT/GA/ENY/08-M06 - Space Based Satellite Tracking and Characterization Utilizing Non-Imaging Passive Sensors
entities.sub: Air Force Institute of Technology thesis, March 2008; the public document that defines 'fastwalker'
entities.desc:
This is the public, distribution-unlimited Department of Defense document that defines the term 'fastwalker' in its own words, and it is on this board because the term reaches the popular literature stripped of that definition. Capt. Bradley R. Townsend, US Army, wrote it at the Air Force Institute of Technology at Wright-Patterson for a Master of Science in Astronautical Engineering, March 2008, DTIC accession ADA478890, APPROVED FOR PUBLIC RELEASE; DISTRIBUTION UNLIMITED.

Section 1.1 gives the definition: 'Satellite based sensors looking down at the Earth's surface occasionally observe reflected light from an object passing through the image which is moving too fast relative to the background of the image to be located within the atmosphere. These objects are commonly called fastwalkers. This term refers to any orbital object seen passing through the field of view of an Earth observing sensor which is suspected of being in orbit.' The word is used 34 times. The words UFO and unidentified do not appear anywhere in the 112 pages. In this document 'fastwalker' is ordinary space-surveillance vocabulary, and the board says so.

What the thesis does supply is a documented pointer. Section 1.2 states that 'In his thesis Osedacz [9] states that a database of fastwalker observations exists with data from as far back as 1972', that Osedacz used data from ballistic missile early warning satellites in geosynchronous orbit and concluded orbit determination for such objects was impossible, and that this 'supported the conclusions of an earlier work conducted by Lem Wong ... The research conducted by Wong is no longer available.' Bibliography entry 9 is 'OSEDACZ, R. Orbit determination of sunlight illuminated objects detected by overhead platforms (M. S. Thesis). 1989.' A 1972-onward detection database and a 1989 predecessor thesis, both named in a public document. Osedacz 1989 is the next document to obtain.

edges.label: the Air Force called Aurora classified after its own department published the figures

sources.name: CIA-RDP90-00965R000807470050-4, Washington Post, 8 February 1985

edges.note: 'Reminded that Aurora has been put in the public domain by the Pentagon, an Air Force spokesman said his orders still were to say only: It's a classified program.' The denial is of disclosability, not of an anomalous craft -- the article's own sources point at Stealth.

timeline.label: Research and Development Board established
timeline.text: The National Security Act of 1947 (61 Stat. 495) creates the Research and Development Board, the statutory coordinating body for defence research. Truman appoints Vannevar Bush its chairman, continuing him from the Joint Research and Development Board the service secretaries had set up after V-J Day.

timeline.label: Project Stork begins
timeline.text: Work begins on Project Stork, designation PPS-100, later carried as contract AF-19741, for the Air Technical Intelligence Center. The first status report of 25 April 1952 describes progress 'from its inception on March 31, 1952'. Seven status reports survive, totalling 107 pages, and the transcribing archive records that further reports referenced in the text are not in NARA custody.

timeline.label: AFR 200-2 puts the release restriction in writing
timeline.text: Air Force Regulation 200-2, short title UFOB, signed by order of the Secretary of the Air Force by N. F. Twining, supersedes AFL 200-5 of 29 April 1952. It designates ATIC as the analysis authority, directs that all evidence be forwarded there, and restricts public discussion to cases conclusively identified as conventional. Identified cases could be discussed; unidentified ones could not.

timeline.label: The FBI investigates Project Winterhaven as possible fraud
timeline.text: An FBI report out of Cincinnati records that Thomas Townsend Brown 'is apparently in Washington attempting to obtain a research and development contract for his so-called Project Winterhaven' and 'anticipates a contract of approximately a million dollars'. The Washington Field Office is directed to determine any possible violation of the Fraud Against the Government statute, and to review Brown's patents at the Patent Office.

timeline.label: An aerospace prime proposes an institute to study gravity
timeline.text: George S. Trimble of the Glenn L. Martin Company writes to Bryce DeWitt that 'our industry was vitally concerned with gravity' and that respectable researchers 'do not wish to get mixed up in the field of gravity research'. He proposes an 'industrial version of the Institute for Advanced Study'. RIAS, Inc. of Baltimore is the result; Louis Witten is its first researcher.

timeline.label: RIAS at the Chapel Hill gravitation conference
timeline.text: The participants list of the conference on the role of gravitation in physics prints 'Witten, L. | RIAS, Inc., Baltimore' and 'Bass, R.W. | RIAS , Inc., Baltimore'. The conference report is WADC Technical Report 57-216, produced under a funding agreement with the Wright Air Development Center. The participants record their own concern to avoid identification with anti-gravity research.

timeline.label: The first DCI asks Congress to investigate
timeline.text: A Worcester Gazette report, filed in CIA records and released in 2014, quotes Adm. Roscoe H. Hillenkoetter, DCI from May 1947 to October 1950: 'The unknown objects are operating under intelligent control. It is imperative that we learn where the UFO's come from and what their purpose is.' He is by then a NICAP board member and has referred his conclusions to the Senate Space Committee.

timeline.label: Corso becomes Chief, Foreign Technology Division, OCRD
timeline.text: Philip J. Corso's own DA Form 66 records him as 'Chief Foreign Technology Div, OCRD USA' from 18 April to 18 July 1962, after a year as a staff officer in the same division. Three months. The same form records him on the Operations Coordinating Board from 1954 to 1957, which his later affidavit describes as membership of the National Security Council.

timeline.label: The 1127th's own history names the recovery pipeline
timeline.text: The 1127th USAF Field Activities Group's semiannual history, doc. AFNIABA 014-67, lists Project BLUE FLY, MIG-17 Exploitation and Project MOON DUST together under FOREIGN MATERIEL PROGRAM. It records exploitation personnel from FTD Detachment 3 deployed to crash sites and about three tons of parts airlifted to Wright-Patterson, and SPADATS notifying the unit of 37 Soviet deorbits.

timeline.label: JANAP 146 still lists UFOs, eight years after Blue Book closed
timeline.text: Change No. 2 to JANAP 146(E) is promulgated. Unidentified flying objects remain a reportable CIRVIS category at Article 201, and Article 208 continues to incorporate 18 U.S.C. 793 and the Canadian Official Secrets Act. Project Blue Book closed in December 1969. The document was released under FOIA on 28 February 1994.

timeline.label: Aurora appears in the Pentagon's unclassified procurement list
timeline.text: The Washington Post reports that the Pentagon's own unclassified P-1 document shows spending on an Air Force programme called Aurora rising from zero to $80 million in FY1986 and $2.27 billion in FY1987. Reminded that its own department had published the figures, an Air Force spokesman said his orders were to say only 'It's a classified program.' Five years before the Aviation Week story.

timeline.label: GAO tells Congress a carve-out contractor lost control of its documents
timeline.text: GAO testifies to the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations that Lockheed reported 1,460 discrepancies in a 40,000-item special-access inventory, 11 of them still unresolved. In the same statement it explains that since 1965 special access programs have been excluded from Defense Investigative Service supervision, and that this is why they are called carve-out contracts.

timeline.label: A public AFIT thesis defines 'fastwalker'
timeline.text: AFIT/GA/ENY/08-M06, distribution unlimited, defines the term in its own words as 'any orbital object seen passing through the field of view of an Earth observing sensor which is suspected of being in orbit'. The words UFO and unidentified appear nowhere in its 112 pages. It names a fastwalker observation database with data from as far back as 1972, and a 1989 predecessor thesis by R. Osedacz.

gaps.text: Robert Sarbacher's alleged consultancy to the Research and Development Board has no primary record. It traces only to Wilbert Smith's handwritten notes of 15 September 1950 and to Sarbacher's own 1983 letter. Carried at Tier 3 on the Sarbacher node; NO edge is drawn to research-development-board.
gaps.wouldClose: The Smith fonds at Library and Archives Canada or the Arthur Bray Fonds at the University of Ottawa. Both refuse this environment.

gaps.text: The 21 November 1950 'Geo-Magnetics' memorandum by Wilbert Smith was not obtained in facsimile. Library and Archives Canada returns 403 or a connection reset on every entry point, the archive.org item some secondary pages link as a scan does not exist, and web.archive.org is unreachable from this environment.
gaps.wouldClose: A facsimile from Library and Archives Canada.

gaps.text: The claim that George Trimble recruited Louis Witten is NOT on the board. The only openable source says Witten approached Bryce DeWitt in a bid to have DeWitt join RIAS, and nothing read states who hired Witten.
gaps.wouldClose: The AIP oral history with Louis Witten of 17 March 2011, which lists both Trimble and RIAS among its topics. repository.aip.org returns 403 to both curl and WebFetch.

gaps.text: The 1127th USAF Field Activities Group's activation and inactivation dates are not carried, and neither is its station. No primary lineage record was found; Fort Belvoir appears only in secondary accounts.
gaps.wouldClose: An Air Force Historical Research Agency lineage and honours statement for the unit.

gaps.text: The 1989 M.S. thesis by R. Osedacz, 'Orbit determination of sunlight illuminated objects detected by overhead platforms', is named in the AFIT 2008 bibliography and has not been obtained. It is the document that would establish the 1972-onward fastwalker database directly rather than through a citation.
gaps.wouldClose: DTIC or AFIT Scholar holding the Osedacz thesis.

gaps.text: The commonly stated chain BDM International to TRW in 1997 and TRW to Northrop Grumman in 2002 was not read off any document. No edge from bdm-international to northrop-grumman is drawn on it, which leaves BDM connected to the board only by its McLean address.
gaps.wouldClose: The 1997 TRW acquisition agreement or a TRW 10-K naming BDM, and the 2002 Northrop Grumman merger documents, from SEC EDGAR.

gaps.text: The P-1 procurement document that carried the Aurora line was not located or read. The chain is a named Washington Post correspondent reporting its contents, in a contemporaneous article preserved in a US government declassified collection.
gaps.wouldClose: The FY1986 Department of Defense Procurement Programs (P-1) exhibit. govinfo does not reach 1985 procurement justification books.

gaps.text: GAO/GGD-83-43 of 18 February 1983, GAO's earlier recommendation on oversight of carve-out contracts which DoD refused, was not opened. It is described on the DIS node only as the 1986 testimony describes it.

GAO/NSIAD-88-2BR, 'Information Security: Actions Taken To Improve Lockheed's Special Access Document Accountability', appeared in a search result only and was not opened. It is the follow-up that would say whether anything changed after 1986. Nothing is cited to it.
gaps.wouldClose: The briefing report itself from gao.gov.

gaps.text: The rename from Sperry Rand Corporation to Sperry Corporation, given by secondary sources as 1 August 1979, has no primary document. EDGAR does not reach back to 1986 filings and no merger agreement or proxy was read.
gaps.wouldClose: A Sperry Corporation filing or proxy predating EDGAR's electronic coverage.

gaps.text: British Patent 300,311, named in two documents Brown authored, was not opened. Espacenet and the UK IPO both refuse this environment.
gaps.wouldClose: The British grant itself from the UK IPO or Espacenet.

gaps.text: The 1956 Aviation Studies (International) report 'Electrogravitics Systems' has no catalogue record anywhere WorldCat indexes. It survives as a reprint whose provenance is one compiler's account of retrieving an unlisted item from one base library. It is on the board at Tier 3 with that stated in the claim text.
gaps.wouldClose: A catalogued holding of the original in any institution.

gaps.text: The May 1985 Advanced Theoretical Physics meeting at BDM rests on papers from a private estate published by a researcher. Neither John B. Alexander's nor Jacques Vallee's published account was read; a named participant in print would move the claim from Tier 3 to Tier 2.
gaps.wouldClose: A published first-person account by a named participant.
